item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Jordan, Egypt condemn Iranian attack on Bahrain - as it happened
item.description:
Iran has targeted airbase in Bahrain in latest resumption of strikes since september

The state-run Bahrain news agency is also carrying the statements of each country in the region responding to Iran’s actions targeting their Gulf neighbour this morning.

Jordan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, and Qatar have all strongly condemned the attack and expressed solidarity with Bahrain.

The Kingdom affirms that the Iranian attacks constitute a violation of international law and the principles of good neighborliness. The Kingdom stresses the importance of an immediate halt to the blatant Iranian attacks on the countries of the region, and of taking serious steps towards achieving security and stability for the countries of the region and their peoples.

The continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that will complicate efforts to contain the tension and undermine political and diplomatic endeavors aimed at achieving security and stability in the region.

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressed the Kingdom of Bahrain’s strongest condemnation of the continued Iranian aggression against its territory, including the attack launched today, Sunday, November 15, 2026, by drones that were intercepted and destroyed by air defense systems in the Kingdom’s airspace.

This comes two days after a similar attack at dawn on Friday, November 13, 2026, by two drones that were also intercepted. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard explicitly claimed responsibility for these attacks. The Ministry praised the efficiency, vigilance, and capability of the Bahrain Defense Force in confronting today’s attack and its complete readiness to deter any aggression.
The Ministry considered these attacks a resumption of Iran’s heinous aggression against the Kingdom and countries in the region, disregarding the provisions of international law and the principles of the UN Charter.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Israel's data shows it allowed half of the promised aid trucks into Gaza
item.description:
Israel's data shows it allowed half of the promised aid trucks into Gaza

Israel has failed to meet its commitments under the Gaza ceasefire deal, allowing in only around half the agreed volume of humanitarian and commercial goods each month since March, Israeli military data shows.

Data obtained by Haaretz newspaper showed a growing shortfall in food deliveries to Gaza, alongside severe shortages of medical supplies, tents and materials to repair damaged infrastructure. Torrential rains have flooded displacement camps, leaving hundreds of thousands of Palestinians in increasingly dire conditions.

Under the ceasefire deal, Israel pledged to allow 4,200 vehicles carrying humanitarian and commercial goods into Gaza each week, equivalent to roughly 18,200 a month.

Deliveries were to include food, fuel, medical supplies and equipment, shelter materials and equipment to repair essential infrastructure.

Data supplied by the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (Cogat) to the US-led International Gaza Support Center (IGSC) show that Israel allowed about 4,700 trucks into Gaza in March, rising to 5,300 in April and more than 9,600 in May.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Mossad abducted Iranian general in Turkey, tortured him for weeks before killing him: Report
item.description:
Mossad abducted Iranian general in Turkey, tortured him for weeks before killing him: Report

Submitted by Elis Gjevori on Sun, 11/15/2026 - 22:06
Israel killed one Iranian general and tortured another, while Israeli strikes on a Lebanese village killed at least 41 people in search for missing Israeli pilot
An Iranian walks over a flag depicting Israel and US during a rally in front of the former US embassy to mark the anniversary of the 1979 Iran hostage crisis, in Tehran on November 4, 2026. (Atta Kenare KENARE/AFP)
Off

Israel kidnapped two Iranian officials and killed one of them in a decades-long search for an Israeli pilot whose fighter jet crashed in Lebanon while bombing the country in 1986, The New York Times reported on Sunday.

Israeli pilot Ron Arad was bombing Lebanese villages in 1986 when one of his missiles malfunctioned, forcing him to eject from his fighter jet.

Since then, Israel has been on a mission to find out what happened to Arad, leaving a trail of death and destruction in its wake which has left more than 40 people dead and dozens more wounded.

The NYT said that the search for Arad was rooted in the "Jewish tradition" to bring its soldiers back to Israel.

In December 2006, Alireza Asgari, a former general in the Quds Force of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), became one of the first victims.

Asgari, who had served as Iran's deputy defence minister, arrived in Istanbul, Turkey and checked into the Ceylan Hotel near Taksim. Shortly afterwards, Mossad agents kidnapped him, the NYT reported.

Years later and after Iran requested information about Asgari's whereabouts, Israeli officials told their US counterparts that they had tortured him for several weeks, believing incorrectly he had information about Arad.

Asgari knew nothing about the Israeli pilot, the Israeli spy agency concluded. Mossad agents killed Asgari anyway and dumped his body in the Black Sea, according to the NYT.

At the time, Meir Dagan headed Mossad. A decision to kill a senior Iranian official would likely have required the Israeli prime minister's approval. Ehud Olmert held that position in 2007.

Iranian officials conducted their own investigation into Asgari's disappearance and found that Israeli agents had broken into his hotel room in Istanbul, drugged and kidnapped him. Investigators also found the vehicle used in the operation abandoned near the Black Sea.

Despite the lack of evidence linking Iran to Arad's disappearance, Israel went on to kidnap General Abdullah Saberi, an IRGC commander, while he was out for a morning run in Damascus in 2021.

Mossad operatives bundled Saberi into a refrigerator box and loaded him into a moving van.

After a lengthy interrogation involving torture, the Israelis dumped Saberi alive in Johannesburg, South Africa, in an attempt to conceal who was behind the kidnapping.

Saberi also knew nothing about Arad.

Turkey and Qatar sign mutual defence agreement
Read More »

A joint Hezbollah-Iranian investigation subsequently concluded that Arad most likely died in 1988 in Nabi Chit, a village in eastern Lebanon, around two years after his plane went down, according to the NYT.

Investigators believed his captors had held him there and later buried him in the village. Israeli officials, however, remained obsessed with the theory that Iran knew what had happened to him.

In December 2025, Israel kidnapped Ahmad Shukr, a retired Lebanese security officer who, according to the NYT, left home to attend what he believed was a business meeting.

Lebanese officials believe Israeli agents abducted him. Shukr has not been seen alive since and his whereabouts are unknown.

Israeli officials now believe that Shukr killed Arad in retaliation for the killing of his brother by Israeli forces near Nabi Chit in 1988.

There is no evidence to support the Israeli theory.

Earlier this year, Israeli forces launched more than 40 strikes on Nabi Chit between 6 and 7 March, believing Arad was buried in a cemetery in the village.

The Israeli attacks killed at least 41 people and wounded more than 40 others, and Arad's body was not found.

Across Lebanon, Israeli attacks have killed at least 4,358 people between 2 March and early September 2026.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
item.description:
In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future

Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.

The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks.

UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.

Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march.

UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police. West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance. The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage.

Tuesday | The work and pensions secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released.

Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia.

Friday | This marks last day of the world’s biggest annual climate conference, Cop31, in Turkey, with final negotiations taking place.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Ma Wee Tin O’Shortbreid: a journey in search of the real Highlands
item.description:
Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid began as a cautionary note: don’t make the Highlands look like a shortbread tin. Then Dougie Wallace shot a Chinese tourist beneath a wee umbrella, and the warning became the title

Growing up in Scotland, our family was one of many who kept their photographs in an old shortbread tin. The lid usually showed a castle beside a loch, a stag, a Highland coo and plenty of tartan. It was always sunny.

Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid is Scots for “my little tin of shortbread”. The title started as a warning to myself: don’t make the Highlands look like a tin of shortbread.

Isle of Mull. Out of the camper van, looking for white-tailed eagles. They were shot to extinction in Britain, the last one in Shetland in 1918. Brought back from Norway in the 1970s. Now they are one of the island’s biggest draws. A bird once shot on sight is part of the sales pitch. The Scotland on the lid promises wilderness and wildlife. The real one comes with binoculars and a long wait.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Delaware hit by rare November tornado
item.description:
Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.

Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba province on Friday, bringing hailstones up to the size of a baseball (about 7.5cm in diameter). Parts of the province recorded up to 73mm of rainfall in just six hours early on Saturday. Such storms are common at this time of year. Water vapour from the Amazon meeting the Andes quickly condenses, resulting in massive cloud formations often associated with heavy downpours, lightning, tornadoes and large hailstones.
